doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Ukraine aid trip and ripples of kindness charity
summary: Left without purpose, she went into Ukraine delivering supplies including forensic equipment, then back in New York started a personal charity of small kindnesses.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: way. But I was like left without purpose. It wasn’t a job that I was giving up, it was a way of life that I had designed to fit all my greatest neuroses and that’s how it worked you know. My need to care for the suffering, my purpose in life, what gave me joy in this world. That’s what gives me happiness. So it’s purely selfish on my part. So Ukraine had just had Russia invade and I think it was five or six months into the war there, the invasion there, and I was so tired of hearing about it I decided I was going to go to Poland and gather the refugee women and children that were now flooding into Poland and start like a 12-step meetings in churches and things to get them to be able to find each other and start creating situations where maybe we could have a work network. I contacted the mayor of Warsaw and I was supposed to meet with him. And when I got there I met a young woman who was driving into Ukraine. We had food for orphans, for the orphanages. The Red Cross was not going into Ukraine. And I was like, “Okay well I’m already here, I’ll just go into Ukraine.” And we drove in and went in to Lviv and there were cafes that were open and magnificent people and musicians playing in the street and I was like this doesn’t feel like war this is incredible. So we started going deeper and deeper into Ukraine and we were given a mission that we couldn’t say where we were going, we had to hand them our driver’s licenses to be photocopied, we had to swear that we were under their law that we couldn’t speak about what we were bringing or who we were bringing it to, and I’d already done, we did gasoline to the front, we’d done protective weaponry like bullet-proof vests, helmets. People were fighting in sneakers, fathers and sons were fighting in sneakers and jeans with kitchen knives. There was no ammunition for a lot of people. It was insane. So we brought this, it turned out that we ended up going to Kiev and we were bringing, which I didn’t know ‘til after, we went into this empty building and there was a smell the likes of which I’ll never forget. I couldn’t even deliver – I couldn’t even bring in the boxes. I had to wait outside and a young man who spoke English brought this older woman in her seventies out to me and he explained to me, ‘cause he spoke English and no one else did and I certainly didn’t speak Ukrainian – even though I found out on that trip that my people were Ukrainian. They were all from the cities in Ukraine. They weren’t Russian. So that was an amazing thing. I was the first family member, after 100 years of escaping, to go back and be on the soil which was very profound, a very spiritual experience happened there. So I found out that we had brought forensic equipment and Merrick Garland was coming to Ukraine the next day to teach them how to document war crimes. And those were the people, the bodies of people that had been at the Mariupol Power Plant underneath. Remember the Russian army wouldn’t let them out. There were 2000 or 3000 people stuck, and people died. They’d been living with the dead before Russia came and took them as prisoners of war. But the bodies that were returned, that they got back, had to be identified for the

loved ones and as war crimes, and that’s the equipment we brought that day, to identify them so their families would know if they were still here or not or if they were in Russian prisoner camps, at the time being tortured. It was insane. But so anyway, talk about feeling a sense of purpose, and because I had no language what I found, all I had to do was hug someone. So this tough woman was going to be identifying bodies. And she was a lioness. She was the most magnificent, youthful, incredible, powerful woman. And when this man was telling me what it was that we were delivering, I started getting tears. And I looked at her and I just hugged her. And this powerhouse of a woman, tough as nails, we started sobbing together. And we did this prayer for the souls. And even though they didn’t understand English, they knew just what we were doing. And it was an amazing experience. And when I got back from Ukraine, I was walking in the streets of New York and there were at least three people for every block that I saw with my antenna for suffering that I saw needed help. And I realized you don’t have to go halfway around the world to do good in this world. It’s right here in front of you. So I started my own little anonymous personal charity just from my own little measly whatever. Because not everything needs money. Sometimes you can see a kid sitting against a building who’s homeless with his little sign and you start talking to him and before you know it you realize he’s a Fentanyl addict, he doesn’t want to be, and by the time the relationship is over he’s going to meetings and he’s in NA and he’s getting sober. That didn’t cost money. You know? Except for the lunch you bought him and maybe the clothes. You know? So I’m just saying that everyone is their own charity and that’s the basis of this. It’s just called ripples of kindness and love. And you do it yourself. And it could be seeing a woman in line for a bus who’s losing her hair and it’s balding on top and you just go up to her and tell her that color of her hair is so fabulous you want to know what she uses, what color is that, what Clairol, and she’ll tell you, “Oh it’s natural,” and she’ll start crying because she was embarrassed to go out, she’s feeling like she’s losing her hair and I’ll tell her how beautiful she is. And before we know it we’re hugging each other. And you know you can change life right here, right in front of you, when you choose. It doesn’t have to be every time, just when you choose, when the spirit calls you to do something nice. Or the guys who clean up the streets now in New York and you go and thank them for their service and say like, “This city is sparkling because of you.” You know “You’re doing such good, thank you.” And you start talking and find out they’re sober nine weeks and you encourage them and you find out what their name is and you know they become people, not this guy cleaning up. You know there are so many little things we can do that don’t take money. But I love doing the things that do take money. I love helping someone in a way that will change their life. So if you know of some way to get donations, because I’ve run out.
